hints: Think about how ammonia behaves when it meets water, does it tend to gain a proton or lose a proton?
Remember ammonia is a familiar weak base, so write its reversible reaction with water to form hydroxide ions.
Consider how much of a weak base reacts and whether water is strong enough to force ammonia to act as an acid.
walkthrough:
**Recall what ammonia does in water**

Ammonia has a lone pair on nitrogen, so it loves to accept a proton. In water it acts as a weak Brønsted-Lowry base.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$$

**Apply weak base idea**

Because it is weak, the equilibrium lies well to the left. That means most nitrogen stays as unreacted $\text{NH}_3$ molecules, with only a small amount converted to $\text{NH}_4^+$ ions.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{weak base = mostly molecules + few ions}$$

**Check if amide ions can form**

To make $\text{NH}_2^-$, ammonia would have to donate a proton and act as an acid. Water is far too weak a base to pull a proton off $\text{NH}_3$, that needs a very strong reagent like sodium metal.

So no $\text{NH}_2^-$ forms in aqueous solution, leaving only $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{NH}_4^+$ present.

options.A: Incorrect. Amide ions, $\text{NH}_2^-$, form only when ammonia acts as an acid with an extremely strong base. Water cannot do this, so no $\text{NH}_2^-$ is present in aqueous ammonia.
options.B: Correct. Ammonia acts as a weak base in water: $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$. The equilibrium lies left, so both unreacted $\text{NH}_3$ molecules and a small amount of $\text{NH}_4^+$ ions are present.
options.C: Incorrect. This ignores the basic reaction of ammonia. Even though ammonia is weak, some molecules do accept protons from water to give $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$, which is why the solution is alkaline.
options.D: Incorrect. This would be true only for a strong base that fully reacts. Ammonia is weak and only partially ionised, so most nitrogen remains as $\text{NH}_3$ molecules, not only $\text{NH}_4^+$.
